newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma issues decree on PM resignation.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma issues decree on PM resignation.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma signed a decree on Wednesday accepting his prime minister's resignation on health grounds, a spokeswoman for Kuchma said.

"The president has signed a decree accepting the resignation of Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, who said he needed medical treatment. His resignation letter says he will be unable to fulfil his duties for two or three months," she said.
Kuchma removed Lazarenko, 44, from his post temporarily on June 19 while he was ill, a move which was widely interpreted as a ploy and as meaning that Lazarenko was being sacked.

Some analysts believe Lazarenko initiated the move so he could depart from power with dignity as Kuchma cannot sack a minister while he is sick. Others say Kuchma feared him as a powerful rival and hesitated to sack him outright.

Deputies in parliament, who will have to approve Kuchma's candidate to replace Lazarenko, said leaders of parliamentary groups were expecting to meet the president for talks on a new candidate at 4 p.m. (1300 GMT).
Several names have been mentioned as potential replacements in local media, including Serhiy Tyhypko, a deputy prime minister with the image of an ambitious young reformer.
The head of Kuchma's administration, Yevhen Kushnaryov, has also been lobbying for Oleh Dyomin, governor of the eastern Kharkiv region, sources close to the administration say.
Anatoly Kinakh, head of the Ukrainian Union of Industrialists and Enterpreneurs, is also said to have a chance.

But nationalist, centrist and liberal deputies said on Wednesday parliament wanted someone "simple", lacking the political ambitions of his predecessor and able to push through reforms to take Lazarenko's place.

The president named Lazarenko's deputy, Vasyl Durdynets, as acting prime minister on June 19 and the deputies said the former police general and Ivan Plyushch, a former parliamentary speaker under Kuchma's predecessor, were their favourites.

At the conservative end of the political spectrum, Interfax-Ukraine news agency quoted the head of the Communist Party, with the biggest number of seats in parliament, as saying they had their own candidate but they would not propose him.

"It is not the prime minister who should be changed, but the political course itself," communist leader Petro Symonenko was quoted as saying. Prominent communist Olexander Tkachenko, first deputy speaker, had been mentioned as a possible candidate.

Symonenko also signalled a fresh battle in parliament, which took six months to pass this year's budget, saying the candidates being proposed by other groups were also "hardly likely to get the communist vote".

Communists, socialists and agrarians have nearly half the seats in parliament but it would be hard for them to stop a concerted move by the rest of the chamber to approve one single candidate proposed by Kuchma.

The president needs backing from 226 deputies in the 450-seat chamber to appoint a new prime minister. Parliament closes in mid-July until September and deputies said they hoped to vote on the new prime minister before they went on holiday.
